terms.definition: A write changes data; a read returns it. Replication treats the two differently.
The point at which a transaction's changes become permanent on a database.
Promoting another copy to take over when the main database fails.

before.note: Read Databases first: replication keeps the transaction and durability promises you learned there across more than one machine. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: A single database is a single point of failure: if its machine dies, the data is unreachable and maybe lost. Replication keeps one or more extra copies of the database on other machines, kept up to date with the first, so a copy can take over if the main one fails and reads can be spread across the copies [[pg-ha]].

The usual shape is one primary that accepts writes and one or more replicas that copy those writes and serve reads. The primary stays the single source of truth for changes; the replicas follow along. PostgreSQL frames this as the standard way to get both high availability and extra read capacity [[pg-ha]].

Replication buys two things: durability and availability, by having copies survive a machine loss, and read scaling, by sending read queries to replicas. It does not by itself let you store more data than one machine holds; that is sharding, a later topic. Replication is about copies of the same data, not splitting it [[mysql-repl]].

terms.definition: The database copy that accepts writes and is the source of truth. Also called the leader or master.
A copy that follows the primary's changes and can serve reads. Also called a follower or standby.
The stream of changes the primary ships to replicas so they can apply the same writes.
Spreading read queries across replicas to handle more read traffic.
Keeping the service up through failures by having a copy ready to take over.

reading.what: Why keeping copies on other machines gives both availability and read capacity.
The primary-and-replica shape and that replicas copy the primary's writes.

canNow: Say why one database is a single point of failure.
Explain what replication gives you and what it does not.

stages.name: How it works
body: The primary records every change in an ordered log and streams it to the replicas, which replay the same changes in the same order. PostgreSQL ships its write-ahead log to standbys; MySQL ships its binary log of events. Either way the replica rebuilds the primary's state by applying the log [[pg-warm-standby]].

Replication can be asynchronous or synchronous. Asynchronous means the primary commits and tells the client done without waiting for replicas, which is fast but means a replica can lag behind. Synchronous means the primary waits for a replica to confirm before telling the client done, which protects against losing that commit on failover but makes every write slower [[pg-ha]].

The gap between a replica and the primary is replication lag. Under asynchronous replication a read sent to a lagging replica can return data slightly out of date, so a user who just wrote something might not see it on the next read if that read hit a behind replica [[mysql-repl]].

When the primary fails, a replica is promoted to be the new primary, a failover. If replication was asynchronous, any writes the old primary had not yet shipped are lost. Setups weigh how much they are willing to lose against how much they are willing to slow every write to avoid it [[pg-warm-standby]].

terms.definition: The primary commits without waiting for replicas; fast, but replicas can lag and a crash can lose recent writes.
The primary waits for a replica to confirm before committing; safer on failover, slower per write.
How far behind the primary a replica is, measured in time or in log position.
Making a replica the new primary, usually during failover.
The ordered record of changes the primary ships to replicas to replay.

reading.what: How a standby replays the primary's log to stay in step.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Reading from replicas introduces a subtle correctness issue: read-your-writes. If you write to the primary and then read from a lagging replica, you may not see your own change. Common fixes are routing a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or waiting for the replica to catch up to the write's log position before reading [[mysql-repl]].

A single-primary design avoids write conflicts, since only one machine accepts writes, but makes the primary a bottleneck and a failure point until a replica is promoted. Multi-primary designs let more than one node accept writes, which removes that bottleneck but creates the problem of two nodes changing the same row at once and having to reconcile the conflict [[mysql-repl]].

Deciding who becomes the new primary safely is itself hard. If two nodes both think they are primary, they can accept conflicting writes, a split brain. Avoiding this needs agreement among the nodes about who leads, which is what consensus algorithms such as Raft provide: a safe, understandable way to elect one leader and keep a single replicated log [[raft-site]].

terms.definition: The guarantee that after you write, your own later reads see that write.
One node takes writes (no conflicts, one bottleneck) versus several (more capacity, write conflicts to resolve).
Two nodes each believing they are primary and accepting conflicting writes.
Nodes agreeing on one value or one leader despite failures; Raft is one algorithm for it.
A majority of nodes that must agree, so two conflicting majorities cannot both form.

reading.what: How a group handles multiple writers and the conflicts that creates.
How a consensus algorithm elects one leader safely, preventing split brain.

canNow: Explain the read-your-writes problem and two fixes.
Say why electing a primary safely needs consensus.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The governing trade-off is the one from the Databases topic made concrete: strong versus eventual consistency. Synchronous replication to a majority gives reads a current view but slows writes and can stall if replicas are unreachable. Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast but lets replicas serve slightly stale reads. Which you choose depends on whether a stale read or a slow write hurts your application more [[pg-ha]].

Replication is also how backups and zero-downtime maintenance work. A standby can be upgraded or taken offline without stopping writes, and failover turns a dead primary into a few seconds of disruption rather than an outage, provided the promotion is handled cleanly and clients reconnect [[pg-warm-standby]].

The hard limit to remember: replication multiplies copies of the same data but never shrinks the data set a single machine must hold. When one machine can no longer hold or write all the data, you must split it, which is Sharding. Replication and sharding are usually combined, each shard being itself replicated [[mysql-repl]].

terms.definition: How sure you are a committed write survives; stronger with synchronous replication, weaker with asynchronous.
A replica kept ready to be promoted, also usable for backups and maintenance.
Upgrading or repairing one copy while others keep serving.
A single shard of a split data set that is itself kept on several replicas.

reading.section: Comparison of Different Solutions, the trade-off table
reading.what: How each replication choice weighs consistency, write speed and failover loss.
Why replication alone does not scale storage, which leads into sharding.

canNow: Choose synchronous or asynchronous replication for a workload and justify it.
Explain how replicas enable backups and maintenance without downtime.
Say why replication does not remove the need for sharding.

misconceptions.myth: A replica is always an exact, up-to-the-moment copy.
misconceptions.truth: With asynchronous replication a replica lags, so a read there can return slightly stale data [[mysql-repl]].

misconceptions.myth: Replication lets you store more data than one machine holds.
misconceptions.truth: It makes copies of the same data; storing more than one machine holds needs sharding [[mysql-repl]].
After an asynchronous failover, writes the old primary had not shipped yet are lost [[pg-warm-standby]].

misconceptions.myth: Any replica can safely decide to become primary.
misconceptions.truth: Without agreement two nodes can both claim to be primary (split brain); safe election needs consensus [[raft-site]].
